RWL2-087-A.title: Which stack heights stay hidden?
RWL2-087-A.prompt: Two nonempty vertical stacks of identical unit cubes stand on the same level, one directly behind the other. The front stack is 4 cubes high. How many different whole-number heights can the back stack have without changing the front silhouette?
RWL2-087-A.hint: Consider the whole-number heights that leave the visible outline four cubes high.

RWL2-194-B.title: Triangles sharing a side
RWL2-194-B.prompt: Mark four points with no three on a straight line. Join each pair. Choose one of the segments. How many triangles with vertices among the four marked points have that entire segment as a side?
RWL2-194-B.hint: The chosen side fixes two vertices. Which marked points could be the third vertex?

RWL2-135-A.title: The bus at the gates
RWL2-135-A.prompt: A bus visits four gates once each. Yellow comes first. Blue comes immediately after Green. Red is exactly two stops after Green. At which stop does the bus reach Blue?
RWL2-135-A.hint: Work backwards from the latest stop Red could occupy.

RWL2-135-B.title: The borrowed books
RWL2-135-B.prompt: Gus, Hiro and Ira each borrow a different book. The books are an atlas, a book of poems and a book about Mars. Gus takes the Mars book. Ira chooses a book with no maps, and the atlas is full of maps. Who takes the atlas?
RWL2-135-B.hint: Cross out the books that Gus and Ira could not have taken.

RWL2-167-D.title: Two unbroken pairs
RWL2-167-D.prompt: Five dancers enter the stage one at a time. Mo enters immediately after Liv. Paz enters immediately after Oli. Nia enters after Liv and before Paz. In which position must Nia enter?
RWL2-167-D.hint: Treat each consecutive pair as a block. Where can Nia enter without splitting either block?

RWL2-185-A.title: Conflicting reports
RWL2-185-A.prompt: Three people describe the same lamp at the same moment. Ira says it was on. Jia says it was off. Kir says both reports are correct. How many of the three reports must be false?
RWL2-185-A.hint: Check the two possible states of the lamp. What happens to the first two reports in each case?

RWL2-226-A.title: The final act
RWL2-226-A.prompt: Four distinct acts perform once each: a choir, a pianist, a drummer and a finale. The finale must be last, and the pianist must perform after the choir. How many running orders are possible?
RWL2-226-A.hint: Ignore the finale for a moment. Pair each order with the order obtained by swapping the choir and the pianist.

RWL2-226-B.title: Switching halls
RWL2-226-B.prompt: Three shows use halls 1, 2 and 3, one show per hall. Last year Art used hall 1, Music used hall 2 and Dance used hall 3. This year every show must change hall. How many complete assignments are possible?
RWL2-226-B.hint: Try each allowable hall for Art. Check the placement of both remaining shows.

RWL2-226-C.title: The matching cards
RWL2-226-C.prompt: Mo, Nia and Oli turn over one card each. One card shows a circle and two cards show triangles. Mo and Oli turn over matching shapes. Who turns over the circle?
RWL2-226-C.hint: Which shape occurs often enough for two cards to match?

RWL2-226-D.title: Which clue is sufficient?
RWL2-226-D.prompt: Tia, Uma, Vik, Wes and Yara fill positions 1 to 5. Vik is third. Uma immediately follows Tia. Which single extra clue would force Uma into fifth position? Enter the clue number. (1) Wes is after Uma. (2) Yara is fifth. (3) Wes is before Yara. (4) Tia is before Vik. (5) Yara is before Tia.
RWL2-226-D.hint: Try the Tia–Uma pair in each possible block of positions. Which clue rules out the earlier block?

RWL2-258-A.title: Orders at four stations
RWL2-258-A.prompt: A torch visits stations A, B, C and D once each. Both A and B must be visited before C. Station D must be visited after C. How many complete routes obey these instructions?
RWL2-258-A.hint: Which stations can change places without breaking an instruction?

RWL2-258-B.title: Joining the line
RWL2-258-B.prompt: Rae, Tia and Uma stand in that order. A newcomer may join at either end or between two people, but Rae and Tia must remain next to one another. How many places can the newcomer take?
RWL2-258-B.hint: Count the gaps in the original line, including both ends. Which gap splits the required pair?

RWL2-258-C.title: The dispatch position
RWL2-258-C.prompt: Five different parcels leave a depot one at a time. The parcel labelled Art must leave before Music, and Music must leave before Maps. The other two parcels can leave at any time. How many different positions can Music occupy?
RWL2-258-C.hint: Bound the position first, then see if each allowed position can actually occur.

RWL2-276-A.title: A false label
RWL2-276-A.prompt: A label says that both coins in a drawer are silver. The label is false. Must the drawer contain at least one coin that is not silver? Answer yes or no.
RWL2-276-A.hint: What would make the original label true?

RWL2-276-B.title: The signal lights
RWL2-276-B.prompt: A true report says that the red light, the blue light or both are on. You can see that the red light is on. Must the blue light be off? Answer yes or no.
RWL2-276-B.hint: Try both possible states of the blue light while keeping the red one on.

RWL2-276-C.title: Five number notices
RWL2-276-C.prompt: An envelope holds a positive whole number. Five notices describe that number: (1) it is even, (2) it is odd, (3) it exceeds 5, (4) it is at most 5, (5) it is a whole number. Whatever number was chosen, what is the total number of true notices?
RWL2-276-C.hint: Look for pairs in which exactly one notice must be true.

RWL2-317-A.title: The missing boxes
RWL2-317-A.prompt: Four boxes labelled Ana, Yara, Zed and Bea all have different weights. An unordered list of the three heaviest reads Yara, Bea, Zed. An unordered list of the three lightest reads Zed, Ana, Yara. Zed is heavier than Yara. Which box is second lightest?
RWL2-317-A.hint: The box missing from each list must occupy an extreme position.

RWL2-349-A.title: Finding a place from a ratio
RWL2-349-A.prompt: Seven runners finish a race, with no ties. Twice as many runners finish behind Bea as finish ahead of her. In which position does Bea finish?
RWL2-349-A.hint: Set Bea aside and split the other runners into the two groups described.

RWL1-006-A.prompt: A solid block of unit cubes measures 5 cubes across, 3 cubes deep and 2 cubes high. How many unit cubes make up the block?

RWL1-009-A.prompt: Two price tags show two-digit numbers. One number has tens digit 2 and units digit A. The other has tens digit B and units digit 8. The two numbers add to 73. Which digit is A?

RWL1-046-A.prompt: A batter scores 83 runs over two innings. The batter scores 9 more runs in the second innings than in the first. How many runs did the batter score in the first innings?

RWL1-052-A.title: Three button presses
RWL1-052-A.prompt: A machine displays 3. Each time you press its button, it doubles the displayed number and then adds 1. What number does it display after three presses?

RWL2-076-A.prompt: A rectangular hall measures 8 m by 5 m. A square porch with sides of 3 m is attached along one full porch edge. How many metres is the perimeter of the combined floor plan?

RWL2-076-B.prompt: A rectangular label measures 8 cm by 5 cm. A 3 cm by 2 cm rectangle is cut from one corner. What is the perimeter of the remaining L-shape in centimetres?

RWL2-104-A.prompt: A turnstile counts each person who enters a pool. Its total is 35 at 8 am, 46 at 9 am and 64 at 10 am. How many people entered between 8 am and 10 am?

RWL2-104-B.prompt: A tank holds 4 litres at noon. At the end of each of the next four hours it holds 13, 20, 35 and 41 litres, in that order. What is the largest increase in any one of those hours, in litres?

RWL2-104-C.title: The covered rainfall reading
RWL2-104-C.prompt: A rain gauge collects 12 mm of rain by noon and 39 mm by 2 pm. Twice as much rain falls in the second hour as in the first. What did the gauge read at 1 pm, in millimetres?

RWL2-114-D.prompt: A locker display has three digit positions. Each position can show any digit from 0 to 9, including a zero at the start. How many displays show exactly two 7s?

RWL2-129-D.title: Meeting on the track
RWL2-129-D.prompt: When the whistle blows, two cyclists set off from the same point on a 180 m circular track. They ride in opposite directions at constant speeds of 7 m/s and 5 m/s. How many seconds pass before they first meet again?

RWL2-145-A.title: Along one cube edge
RWL2-145-A.prompt: A large cube is built from unit cubes, eight along each edge. Look only at the eight unit cubes along one marked edge. How many of those eight contain a corner of the large cube?

RWL2-163-C.prompt: Six stacks of unit cubes stand in two rows of three. Five of the stacks are each 3 cubes high. The six stacks contain 22 cubes altogether. How many cubes high is the sixth stack?

RWL2-173-A.title: Visitors per hour
RWL2-173-A.prompt: A visitor counter at a gallery shows 14 at 10 am and 35 at 1 pm. On average, how many visitors entered per hour during that time?

RWL2-174-A.title: Before the water was drawn
RWL2-174-A.prompt: A gardener draws one fifth of the water from a tank. The tank now holds 32 litres. How many litres did it hold before the gardener drew any water?

RWL2-311-B.prompt: Two runners travel in the same direction at constant speeds of 6 m/s and 4 m/s. The faster runner catches the slower runner 18 seconds after setting off. How many metres apart were they when the faster runner set off?

RWL2-331-D.prompt: A parallelogram banner has area 96 cm². Join the midpoints of its four sides in order to form an inner parallelogram. Join the midpoints of that inner parallelogram to form a second one. How many square centimetres lie inside the first midpoint parallelogram but outside the second?

RWL2-349-C.prompt: Three bags contain different numbers of marbles, chosen from 2, 3, 5 and 7. The bags hold 12 marbles altogether. The yellow bag contains fewer marbles than either of the other two. How many marbles are in the yellow bag?

RWL1-001-B.hint: Mark positions 1 to 6 on one repeat. Which position in the pattern do tiles 6 and 12 share?

RWL1-002-C.hint: Draw the extra columns beside the original rectangle. Then draw the new rows across the enlarged width. Which tiles sit in the new corner?

RWL1-003-D.hint: Draw one filled tin. Mark the mass of the tin separately from the clay before reversing what was removed.

RWL1-004-D.hint: Choose the thousands digit first. In the last two positions, which pairs of unused cards form a multiple of four?

RWL1-005-D.hint: Make separate tallies for the units, tens and hundreds places. In each column, count only tickets the printer actually labels.

RWL1-006-D.hint: Sketch the three tunnels crossing at the middle cube. How many new cubes does the second tunnel remove? What about the third?

RWL1-008-C.hint: Write the two middle digits as matching boxes. Which multiple of 9 could equal 10 plus twice the boxed digit?

RWL1-009-D.hint: The first digit of BCD is nonzero. Which hundreds digits can three two-digit numbers reach? Test the smallest legal AB first.

RWL1-010-C.hint: Write each number in tens and ones before adding them. How could you count a pair just once?

RWL1-011-C.hint: Factor 216 into primes. Which exponents must change for the quotient to be a square, and how little can you remove?

RWL1-012-D.hint: After you fix the tile covering cells 5 and 6, sketch the cells left on each side. How can you combine one tiling of each side?

RWL1-013-D.hint: After dividing out the highest common factor, could the two smaller numbers share any prime? List the factor pairs that pass that check.

RWL1-015-C.hint: Shift the lowest and highest numbers by the same amount as the candidate. Which multiples belong to that new interval, including its ends?

RWL1-017-D.hint: Draw a rectangle enclosing both cells. Would it have appeared once or twice if you added the two single-cell counts?

RWL1-018-C.hint: Write down the number of slips and their total before and after one merge. How often must you repeat that change?

RWL1-019-D.hint: Treat each side of the gap as its own board. Find an upper bound for one side, then draw dominoes to see whether it can be attained.

RWL1-020-D.hint: Write the first few powers of 7 as last digits. What information about the exponent determines the position in that cycle?

RWL1-024-D.hint: The total number of seedlings stays fixed. Can you divide the total into equal parts so both the old and new ratios use whole numbers of those parts?

RWL1-026-D.hint: Draw seven boxes for the days. Bracket days 1–5 above them and days 4–7 below them. What does the extra amount represent when you add the two group totals?

RWL1-027-D.prompt: One type of packet contains 12 biscuits, a third of them ginger. A second type also contains 12 biscuits, half ginger. The ginger biscuits must make up exactly 17/42 of all the biscuits in a box. What is the least number of whole, unopened packets it can contain?
RWL1-027-D.hint: How many ginger biscuits does each whole packet contribute? Compare the two packet counts with the required fraction of the box.

RWL1-030-D.hint: Mark both starting offsets on one timeline, then locate the first shared beat. The repeat period tells you how far from there to the next shared beat.

RWL1-033-B.hint: Make two rows, one with Finn truthful and one with Finn lying. In each row, decide whether the whole claim about different types must be true or false.

RWL1-038-D.hint: Fix the two blank answers. If an attempted answer changes from wrong to correct, what happens to the penalty as well as the four points earned?

RWL1-040-D.hint: Write a letter for each bag. Across the four three-bag weighings, how many times does each letter appear? Which weighing leaves out the heaviest bag?

RWL1-041-C.hint: Compare one short drill exchanged for one long drill. Then add both sessions: how many copies of one short-plus-long pair do you get?

RWL1-045-C.hint: Work out how many grams the gap between the top chambers loses each minute. Check that both still contain sand at the time you find.

RWL1-054-D.hint: Make a table with move number, square and next direction. A return to the same square completes a loop only if the direction also matches.

RWL1-059-A.hint: Label the markers 1 through 5 and write only the terms whose marker numbers the question includes.

RWL1-062-A.hint: If a display has no cloud, which symbols remain available in each window? Compare that count with all possible displays.

RWL2-069-B.prompt: Seven singers are available for a duet. Three know the harmony part. A pair qualifies if at least one of its singers knows that part. How many different pairs qualify? Count the singers chosen, regardless of which part each sings.
RWL2-069-B.hint: Which pairs would have to be left out of a list of all possible duets?

RWL2-081-B.prompt: Two paths of equal length run from a beacon to two posts. The paths and the straight line between the posts form a triangle. The inside angle at one post is 26°. What is the angle at the beacon, in degrees?

RWL2-082-A.prompt: A grid has 5 columns and 7 rows. A horizontal seam follows a grid line with 2 rows below it. How many grid-line rectangles have part of their interior above the seam and part below?
RWL2-082-A.hint: Sketch the seam. Which horizontal lines can be the bottom and top of a rectangle that crosses it?

RWL2-100-C.prompt: A rail network has 4 red stations and 4 blue stations. Each red station links to every blue station. Only opposite colours are linked. Starting at a specified red station, take two moves without revisiting the start. How many different ordered routes are possible?

S001.intro: Put 14 beads into groups of five and four beads stay loose. What happens to the loose beads if you add another full group? This leftover is the remainder.

example.prompt: You have 29 beads. If you lay them in rows of five, how many are in the unfinished row?
steps: Set aside five full rows. They use 5 × 5 = 25 beads.
Four beads remain because 29 − 25 = 4. Adding another five beads would make one more full row and leave the same four loose.

S001.bridge: In the repeating row of symbols, where does an exact multiple of six land? Look for what a remainder of zero tells you about the final symbol.

S002.intro: Adding a column of squares changes a rectangle’s area by the height of that column. You can work with a tidy rectangle first, then add or remove one strip to get the exact area.

example.prompt: What is 31 × 8?
steps: Split the array after column 30. The blue rectangle has 30 columns with eight squares in each, giving 30 × 8 = 240 squares.
The gold column contributes eight more squares. The entire array has 240 + 8 = 248.

S002.bridge: The film uses a rectangle that is too wide instead. Watch which strip has to come off, and why its whole area matters.

S003.intro: At the end of a number machine you know the output. Ask which operation produced it. Undo that operation first, then follow the arrows back to the input.

example.prompt: A number is increased by 3 and then doubled. The result is 22. What was the number?
steps: Work back from 22. The last arrow doubles the middle number, so the middle box must contain 22 ÷ 2 = 11.
The first arrow adds 3. The starting box therefore holds 11 − 3 = 8. Run the machine forwards to check that (8 + 3) × 2 = 22.

S003.bridge: Follow one pile of tickets through the stations. As you rewind each station, ask what the pile held just before that change.
S003.recap: Start with the known finish. Undo the changes in reverse order. If some fraction was removed, identify the fraction left and use it to recover the whole. Replay the changes forwards to check.

S004.headline: Which place has the fewest choices?
S004.intro: A zero in the middle of 306 is useful. Put the zero first and 036 represents just 36. When you arrange digit cards, reserve any restricted places before filling the gaps.

example.prompt: Three cards show 0, 3 and 8. Use every card once. How many three-digit numbers have the 3 at one end?
steps: If 3 is first, the other two cards can sit in either order. The numbers are 308 and 380.
If 3 is last, 0 cannot go first. Only 803 works. The two cases give 2 + 1 = 3 numbers altogether.

S004.bridge: In the harder question, the first digit decides the size of the number while the last two decide divisibility by four. Which choices can you rule out before arranging the remaining cards?

S005.intro: A printer uses two copies of the digit 5 to print a single ticket numbered 55. Before starting a tally, decide what one tally mark should stand for.

example.prompt: Tickets are numbered from 48 through 58. How many tickets contain a 5? How many copies of the digit 5 does the printer use?
steps: The tickets from 50 through 58 each contain a 5. There are nine such tickets. Neither 48 nor 49 contains one.
The tens column contributes nine fives. Ticket 55 supplies one more in its units column. That makes ten printed fives on nine tickets.

S005.bridge: Watch the film tally one place-value column at a time. When a number qualifies in two columns, decide whether the question calls for one mark or two.

S006.intro: Think of lifting off the top floor of a cube building. A stack three cubes high leaves a square on each of three floor plans, even when you cannot see it from the front.

example.prompt: Three solid stacks stand side by side on a table. Their heights are 1, 2 and 2 cubes. How many cubes are there?
steps: Start at the table. All three stacks reach the bottom level, but only the second and third stacks reach the next level.
The floor counts give 3 + 2 = 5 cubes. Adding the stack heights gives 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 as well. Each little cube belongs to one floor and one stack.

S006.bridge: When the tunnel meets the vertical shaft, which cube appears in both plans for removal? Follow it on the middle floor before subtracting.

example.prompt: A two-digit number has 2 tens and an unknown units digit A. Adding 7 gives 31. What is A?
steps: The units must end in 1. Since A + 7 is between 7 and 16, the only possible total ending in 1 is 11.
This makes A = 4. The 11 units supply one ten and one unit, and 24 + 7 = 31.

S009.intro: In a letter sum, AB represents a number with A tens and B ones. Every appearance of A represents the same digit. When two ones digits add to ten or more, carry one ten into the next column.
S009.recap: Write the units digit and mark the carry above the tens column. When the sum of two two-digit numbers has three digits, the hundreds digit must be 1. Put the completed numbers back into the original sum and check the rules about different letters.
S009.bridge: In the film, follow the ten ones when two numbers ending in 5 are added. Which column receives the extra ten? Later, what does the hundreds digit tell you before you try a single tens digit?

example.prompt: A water meter records how many litres have passed through a pipe. It reads 11 L at minute 2 and 23 L at minute 5. What is the average flow rate during that interval?
steps: The volume increases by 23 − 11 = 12 L. The elapsed time is 5 − 2 = 3 minutes.
The average flow rate is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 litres per minute. The flow could have varied within those three minutes.

S045.bridge: The fastest rise on the film’s chart is measured in units per minute. On the price graph, the crossing has two coordinates. Which coordinate gives a number of visits, and which gives the cost?

example.prompt: Everyone in this puzzle either always tells the truth or always lies. Bo always lies and says, “Mira always lies.” Which kind of speaker is Mira?
steps: Bo’s claim is false, so Mira cannot be someone who always lies.
The puzzle allows exactly two types. The remaining possibility is that Mira always tells the truth.

S068.bridge: Kai says both people are liars. If Kai lies, does that force both parts of his claim to be false? Try one true part and one false part before moving to the four-speaker puzzle.
S068.recap: Judge the whole sentence. A claim joined by “and” is true only if both parts are true. One false part makes the whole claim false. Once you have assigned the speakers’ types, test every sentence again.

example.prompt: Two square tiles, each 2 cm on a side, meet along one complete edge. How long is the outside boundary of the joined shape?
steps: The two loose tiles have 8 cm of perimeter each. The shared edge contributes 2 cm from each tile to that total.
Remove those two contributions to get 16 − 4 = 12 cm. The joined shape is a rectangle measuring 4 cm by 2 cm.

S076.bridge: Trace two loops on the board with the hole, one around the outside and one around the opening. When the corner comes off, match each lost edge with a newly exposed edge.

example.prompt: A lunch order is either one sandwich on its own or one soup with one roll. There are three sandwiches, two soups and two rolls to choose from. How many different lunches are possible?
steps: There are three sandwich lunches. Each of the two soups can go with either of two rolls, making four soup lunches.
The two groups do not overlap. Adding 3 and 4 gives seven lunches.

S079.bridge: Make a row for each permitted arrangement of colours in the exhibit rooms. Mark which rows allow B and which positions can hold A before multiplying choices.

example.prompt: The larger of two bowls holds four more cherries than the smaller. It also holds twice as many as the smaller. How many cherries are in the two bowls altogether?
steps: Draw the smaller bowl as one bar. The larger bowl can be drawn as two copies of it. The extra bar represents four cherries.
The bowls hold 4 and 8 cherries, making 12 in all. Both the four-cherry difference and the two-to-one comparison fit.

figure.alt: One equal bar represents the smaller bowl. Two bars of the same length represent the larger bowl. Its extra bar is labelled 4 cherries.

S095.intro: A difference can give you the size of an unknown part. Draw a bar for each amount and use the second clue to work out what the extra piece represents.

example.prompt: A gallery has just three rooms, A, B and C. The only doorways are A–B and B–C. You start in A and walk to B. If you may never revisit a room, where can you go next?
steps: The doors from B lead to A and C. Cross out A because you already visited it.
C is the only legal next stop. Without a record of the earlier room, both doors might look available.

example.prompt: Which unordered pairs of different positive integers add to 8?
steps: Write the smaller number first. Values 1, 2 and 3 give (1,7), (2,6) and (3,5).
Using 4 would require (4,4), which breaks the different-number rule. A larger first number would merely reverse a pair already listed.

example.prompt: A bowl holds two plums and one pear. Pick two pieces without replacement, choosing each remaining piece with equal probability. What is the probability that both are plums?
steps: The chance of a plum first is 2/3. After that plum is taken, just one of the two remaining pieces is a plum.
Follow the two successful draws. Their probability is (2/3) × (1/2) = 1/3.

example.prompt: A robot moves forward one or two tiles at a time. Five routes reach tile 4 and eight reach tile 5 from the same start. How many routes to tile 5 skip tile 4?
steps: Every route that visits tile 4 has exactly one way to continue to tile 5. Those five routes form one final-step group.
The remaining 8 − 5 = 3 routes must finish by jumping directly from tile 3. Working backwards recovers the missing group without listing all eight routes.

example.prompt: A robot must move exactly four spaces forward. Each move may be 1, 2 or 3 spaces, but consecutive moves must have different lengths. List all possible move sequences.
steps: Start with 1. The next move can be 3 to finish, or 2 followed by 1. Starting with 2 leaves two spaces, which would require either another 2 or two consecutive 1s.
Starting with 3 forces a final 1. The complete list is (1,3), (1,2,1) and (3,1). Sorting by the first move shows that no sequence is missed.

example.prompt: A machine starts at 8 before any button presses. Successive presses display 5, 2, 6, 2 and 6. After that the display keeps alternating between 2 and 6. After which press does it first enter the loop?
steps: The first press gives 5. The second gives 2, and the third gives 6.
The fourth press repeats the state from press 2. The loop is 2, 6, so the machine first enters it on press 2. The earlier 8 and 5 never recur.

example.prompt: Every path in a network joins a red station to a blue station. A walker starts at a red station and takes three paths. What colour must the final station be?
steps: After one path the walker is at blue, after two at red, and after three at blue.
Each pair of moves returns to the starting colour. Any odd number of moves from red ends at blue.

example.prompt: A number of flags from 15 to 40 inclusive is one flag short of complete rows of 3 and of complete rows of 4. Which counts are possible?
steps: Add one flag. The adjusted count must be divisible by both 3 and 4, so it is a multiple of 12 between 16 and 41.
The adjusted counts are 24 and 36. Removing the extra flag gives 23 and 35. Both meet the two remainder clues and fall in the original interval.

example.prompt: In triangle ABC, angle A is 40° and angle B is 60°. Extend side BC past C to a point D. What is the exterior angle ACD?
steps: The interior angle ACB is 180° − 40° − 60° = 80°.
Rays CB and CD point in opposite directions, so ACB and ACD complete a straight angle. The exterior angle is 180° − 80° = 100°.

example.prompt: Three different positive whole numbers sum to 9. What is the greatest possible value of the smallest number?
steps: If the smallest were at least 3, the next two would be at least 4 and 5. The sum would be at least 12, exceeding 9.
The numbers 2, 3 and 4 sum to 9 and attain a smallest number of 2. The bound and this example prove 2 is the maximum.

example.prompt: Two positive whole numbers sum to 7. How many different pairs are there if swapping their order counts as the same pair?
steps: Write the smaller number first. A smaller number of 4 or more would make the sum at least 8.
First numbers 1, 2 and 3 give (1,6), (2,5) and (3,4). The larger partner is forced each time, giving exactly three pairs.

example.prompt: Three identical square tiles each have perimeter 8 cm. They form an L shape, with two complete edge joins and no overlaps. What is the perimeter of the L?
steps: Each tile has side length 2 cm. The three separate perimeters add to 24 cm.
Each of the two joins hides a 2 cm edge on both tiles that meet there. Remove 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm, leaving 16 cm of outside boundary.

example.prompt: Each speaker always tells the truth or always lies. Sue says, “Tom is a liar.” Tom says, “Uri is a liar.” Must Sue and Uri have the same type?
steps: If Sue tells the truth, Tom lies. If Sue lies, Tom tells the truth. Sue and Tom have opposite types in both cases.
Tom’s statement gives the same opposite-type relationship with Uri. Reversing type twice brings us back to Sue’s type, so Sue and Uri must match.

example.prompt: A pattern starts at 4 and doubles at each step. Add the first four terms, then compare their sum with the fifth term. How much larger is that fifth term?
steps: The first four terms total 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 60. The doubling rule gives the next term as 64.
The gap is 64 − 60 = 4. More generally, when a finite doubling sum is doubled and the original sum is subtracted, the middle terms cancel, leaving the next term minus the first.

example.prompt: A two-digit number has 6 tens and units digit A. Subtracting 27 gives 38. Which digit is A?
steps: Undo the subtraction to recover the whole number. It is 38 + 27 = 65, so A is 5.
Check in columns. Regroup 65 as 5 tens and 15 units. Subtracting 2 tens and 7 units leaves 3 tens and 8 units.

example.prompt: Select three distinct whole numbers from 1 through 6 with sum 10. Find every set by fixing its two smallest members first.
steps: With smallest 1, the second cannot be 2 because the third would be 7. The second can be 3 or 4, giving (1,3,6) and (1,4,5). From second 5 onward the third would be smaller.
With smallest 2, second 3 gives (2,3,5). Second 4 already gives a repeated 4. A smallest member of at least 3 would force a sum of at least 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. The three listed sets are complete.

example.prompt: A fair coin picks bag A on heads and bag B on tails. Bag A contains two red tokens. Bag B contains one red and one blue token. Draw one token uniformly from the selected bag. What is the probability of red?
steps: The chance of choosing A and then red is (1/2) × 1 = 1/2. The chance of choosing B and then red is (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4.
These two routes are disjoint. Add their probabilities to obtain 3/4.

example.prompt: A box contains six pieces. Each is a square, a circle or a triangle. There are two triangles and equal numbers of squares and circles. How many circles are in the box?
steps: Set the two triangles aside. All four remaining pieces must be squares or circles.
The two groups have the same size, so each has 4 ÷ 2 = 2 pieces. There are two circles.

example.prompt: Two chimes sound together at minute 0. The first sounds every 4 minutes, and the next time they sound together is minute 12. Could the second chime sound every 2 minutes?
steps: At minute 4 the first would sound again, and a chime with a two-minute interval would already sound for the second time after its start.
They would meet at minute 4, contradicting the first repeat at minute 12. A two-minute interval is impossible.

example.prompt: Four nonempty cube stacks fill a 2-by-2 base. The row maxima from front to back are 3 and 1. The column maxima from left to right are also 3 and 1. What is the least possible total number of cubes?
steps: The back-row and right-column maxima of 1 force all three stacks in those positions to have height 1. Only the front-left stack can attain height 3.
Build the front row with heights 3 and 1, and the back row with heights 1 and 1. Both sets of maxima fit. The forced heights total six cubes.

S008.intro: Write 6, 0 and 3 in the first three boxes of a five-digit palindrome. Reading from either end must give the same digits. Which boxes belong to the same pair, and which digit has no partner?
S008.bridge: When the film divides 2772 by 11, pause before the calculation. How much do the two 2s contribute together? What about the two 7s?
S008.recap: In a five-digit palindrome, the first and last digits match, as do the second and fourth. Count each pair twice in the digit sum and the centre once. Check whether zero is allowed in each position.

example.prompt: A five-digit palindrome starts with 60 and has a 3 in the middle. What fills the last two places?
steps: The second box holds 0. Its partner, the fourth box, must also hold 0. The middle 3 stays in place.
The first box holds 6, so put 6 in the last box. Read 60306 from either end to check the five digits.

S010.headline: How far does a reversal move a number?
S010.intro: In 23, the 2 stands for twenty. In 32, the same digit stands for two. Track what each digit gains or loses when it changes place, then combine the changes.

example.prompt: How much larger is 32 than 23? Explain the change by following the two digits.
steps: The 3 gains 27 when it moves from 3 to 30. The 2 loses 18 when it moves from 20 to 2.
The gain is 9 more than the loss. For tens digit A and units digit B, the reversed number minus the original is 9 × (B − A). Its sign tells you which number is larger.

S010.recap: For a reversal, keep the subtraction in the order the question gives. For a letter sum, mark each carry. Finally, put the digits back into every position and check any restrictions on zero or repeated digits.
S010.bridge: When the film swaps 26 and 62, which digit gains the most value? In the final addition, pause at the first candidate: its sum is correct, but which two letters would have to share a digit?

S011.intro: Factor 50 as 2 × 5 × 5. To make two identical whole-number factors, put one 5 on each side. What happens to the 2? Tracking each copy of a prime will tell you which numbers are squares.
S011.bridge: The film finds the smallest multiplier that turns 2016 into a square. Which prime factors have an unpaired copy? Explain why a smaller multiplier cannot complete both pairs.
S011.recap: To list divisors, choose how many copies of each prime to take. Choosing no copies gives 1. To recognise a square, check that every prime occurs an even number of times. To test whether a number greater than 1 is prime, try prime divisors up to its square root.

example.prompt: Why is 50 not a square even though two of its prime factors are fives?
steps: Try to split 2 × 5 × 5 into two identical groups. Give each group one 5. The single 2 has no partner.
One more 2 would make two equal groups. Indeed, 2 × 50 = (2 × 5) × (2 × 5) = 100.

S012.headline: Which earlier values do you need?
S012.intro: Some rules use the last value. Others need two earlier values. Write down exactly which values the rule uses and circle the given starting values before you calculate.

example.prompt: A sequence begins with 2 and 5. Each new term is the sum of the previous two. What is the fifth term?
steps: Term 3 uses both starting values, so it is 2 + 5 = 7. For term 4, move one place along and add 5 + 7 = 12.
Term 5 is 7 + 12 = 19. Read back the five terms, 2, 5, 7, 12, 19. Each term after the first two is the sum of the two terms immediately before it.

S012.bridge: Pause when the film marks rung 3 as broken. Is rung 4 still reachable? Trace its possible final jumps before the film fills in the table.

S013.intro: Two bells can ring together again, and two ribbons can be cut into equal pieces. In one problem the answer must be a multiple of both numbers. In the other it must divide both numbers. Which way does the division go?

example.prompt: A 12 cm ribbon and a 20 cm ribbon must be cut into equally long whole-centimetre pieces with no waste. What is the greatest possible length of a piece?
steps: A piece length that fits both ribbons also fits the leftover 8 cm when 12 is taken from 20. It must also fit the 4 cm left when 8 is taken from 12.
The length therefore divides 4, and 4 itself works: three pieces make 12 cm and five make 20 cm. A piece can be at most 4 cm long.

S013.bridge: The film first times two activities, then packs red and blue markers. In which example must the answer divide both starting numbers? In which must both numbers divide the answer?

S015.bridge: When the film adds 1 to make a number divisible by both 4 and 6, pause. Where must the two ends of the search interval move? After finding a common multiple, how will you get back to the original number?

example.prompt: A jar leaves 5 counters loose when you make groups of 7. What is the smallest number of counters to add so no counters are loose?
steps: A full group needs 7 counters. The unfinished group already has 5, so add 7 − 5 = 2.
Try two different jar sizes to check the rule: 12 becomes 14, and 19 becomes 21. The full groups already in the jar never need to change.

S017.bridge: In the film’s marked grid, first count rectangles containing cell A. To remove the unwanted ones, which four boundary choices guarantee a rectangle contains both A and B?

example.prompt: The drawing has two square cells in one row. Use the three numbered lines to name every rectangle, including squares.
steps: The top and bottom edges are fixed. Lines 1 and 2 bound the left square. Lines 2 and 3 bound the right square.
Lines 1 and 3 enclose the whole strip. These are all three pairs of distinct vertical lines, so there are exactly 3 rectangles.

S018.intro: If a move changes a score by an even number, its odd-or-even status stays the same. If every move changes the score by an odd number, that status flips each time. Try to predict what happens after two moves.

example.prompt: A counter starts on 8 and moves either 2 or 4 places right each turn. Can it land on 15?
steps: Both jumps add whole pairs, so the counter starts even and stays even after each jump.
The target 15 is odd. That rules it out, regardless of the order or number of jumps.

S018.bridge: When the film merges two entries into their sum plus 1, watch two totals: how many entries remain, and what all the entries add to. Which of these tells you how many moves are left?

S019.bridge: In the film’s first 4-by-4 example, the crosses mark the two leftmost squares in the top row. Which domino covers the two top squares that remain? What would you have to change if the middle two had been removed instead?

example.prompt: Five squares in one row are coloured blue, gold, blue, gold, blue. Could edge-to-edge dominoes cover the strip completely?
steps: The row has three blue squares and two gold squares. A domino over any pair of neighbours uses one of each colour.
There are only two gold squares, so at most two dominoes can fit. Even when both fit, a blue square stays uncovered.

S019.recap: To show a covering is impossible, compare the available colours with what each domino needs. To show a covering exists, describe the actual placements. If the middle two squares of the film’s top row are removed instead, cover each top corner and the square immediately below it with a vertical domino. Cover the middle two squares of row 2 with one horizontal domino. Each of the two full lower rows takes two horizontal dominoes.

S020.bridge: For the sum in the film, 12 complete blocks use exponents 1 to 48. The next exponent is 49: which position is that in the repeating pattern of last digits?

example.prompt: A sign repeats the four readings 1, 2, 3, 4, beginning with 1. What does it show on the 12th reading?
steps: Readings 1–4 make the first full block. Readings 5–8 make the second, and 9–12 the third.
The 12th reading is the last one in its block, so it shows 4. Reading 13 then goes back to 1.

S020.recap: Number the positions in a cycle from 1. A multiple of the cycle length lands on the last position. In a sum, add the contribution of every full block before the tail. An exponent keeps increasing even when its last-digit position goes back to 1.

S022.intro: One half of a box depends on what is in it when you take that half. Sketch a line for the starting pile. After the first removal, draw a bracket around the part that the next fraction describes.
S022.bridge: When the second class takes half the chalk that is left, pause. Which pieces belong inside the new whole? In the final puzzle, which change would you undo first?

example.prompt: Three different photos show a cat, an owl and a fox. The cat and owl photos must be beside each other. How many rows can you make?
steps: Clip the cat and owl photos together. The fox can go to the left or to the right of the clip.
For either position of the fox, the pair can read cat–owl or owl–cat. That gives 2 × 2 = 4 different rows.

S023.bridge: In the five-badge puzzle, first count the rejected rows in which A touches B. Which of them will be counted a second time when you count rows in which C touches D?

S024.recap: Label the two quantities in order. A ratio compares one group with the other. To find a fraction of the whole, count every group in the denominator. When items move between groups, the total number of items stays fixed even when the number of ratio parts changes.

S025.bridge: When the two teams have different numbers of attempts, put their results over a common denominator. In the price puzzle, which price is the base for the second change?
S025.recap: Write the base amount beside each percentage. To compare two rates, use equal denominators. For two successive price changes, apply the second multiplier to the price after the first change.

S026.bridge: The film uses two overlapping lists: the first four readings and the last three of a list of six. Mark their positions from 1 to 6. Which reading contributes to both totals?

S027.bridge: In the final card puzzle, imagine giving every item the lower marking rate first. What extra share does each item in the higher-rate group then contribute?

S029.bridge: In the film, the final price is $360 after a 25% sale. What fraction of the price immediately before the sale is $360? Rebuild that price before undoing the earlier increase.
S029.recap: A discount of 30% leaves 70% of the old amount. To recover the old amount, divide what remains by 0.7. If asked for a percentage increase from the reduced price, measure the increase against that reduced price.

S030.intro: A flash marks one instant on a timeline. The gap between two flashes is a length of time. Mark the start and finish, and check whether an event at either boundary counts.
S030.bridge: The film’s sensor waits 35 seconds before its first flash. The two signals in the next puzzle both flash at time zero. How does that change the first mark on each timeline?

S031.bridge: After the pumps have run for two minutes, the film opens a leak. Sketch a line at that instant. How much water is already in the tank, and which rates apply only after the line?
S031.recap: Write each rate as work per unit of time. Add rates that move the work forward and subtract any that undo it. When the rate changes, start the next interval with the work already completed.

S033.bridge: Ava says she is a liar. Try each possible type and check whether her sentence fits. In the later four-person puzzle, can two linked claims force a type before you guess anyone’s identity?

S034.bridge: On the film’s out-and-back ride, the distance counter stops for twelve minutes. Does the elapsed-time counter stop too? Decide which total belongs under the total distance.
S034.recap: Put the distance and elapsed time for every leg in the same units. A stop adds time and zero distance. Divide the trip’s total distance by its total elapsed time to find the average speed.

S036.bridge: Pause when the film places a sideways domino in the top-left corner of the two-row board. Which square would be trapped unless the next domino went directly underneath it?
S036.recap: Trace a finished tiling from the left. Each new column begins with either an upright domino or two sideways dominoes stacked together. On a two-row strip those choices make different tilings, and every tiling can be read back this way.

S037.bridge: Start a second clock when the chasing runner sets off. What gap has already opened? In the round-track puzzle, which clock does the question use for the second meeting?
S037.recap: Measure the gap when both movers are in motion. On a loop, identify the relative distance needed for one meeting: a lap gained in a same-direction chase, or a lap of combined movement in opposite directions. Count the requested meeting and read the correct clock.

S038.bridge: In the film’s ticket office, there are 24 tickets in all. If x are adult tickets, why can 24 − x stand for the child tickets? Write a money total and check the units of each term.
S038.recap: Say what the unknown measures and attach a unit. A ticket count plus another count gives tickets. A price times a count gives money. Substitute your answer into each original condition.

S039.bridge: The rider covers 30 km each way at different speeds. Which leg takes more time? Add the stop to the elapsed time before you decide what distance belongs in the numerator of the average.
S039.recap: An average speed is total distance divided by elapsed time. On a stop, time increases while distance stays fixed. To reach a target average, compare the actual and target distances after the same amount of time.

S040.bridge: Add the two shop orders in the film before trying to find either price. How many identical notebook-and-ruler pairs can you see? In the box puzzle, how many times does each box appear across the three weighings?

S041.bridge: In the pen-and-marker puzzle the film doubles a whole shopping order. Which items and which price must double before the markers can cancel?

S043.bridge: Compare the film’s corner cut with its enclosed window. Trace each old edge that disappears and each cut edge that appears. Which change adds to the total boundary?
S043.recap: When two pieces join along a whole side, that side was present in both separate perimeters. Remove it twice. For a cut, compare the old and new edges directly. Trace an enclosed hole separately if its boundary is asked for.

S044.intro: Start at the known end of a chain of changes. Ask what the last step did, undo it, and then work back one step at a time. If the story counts whole objects, discard any result that would require part of an object.
S044.bridge: The film’s last machine finishes with a two-digit reading in a stated range. Which reverse step requires exact division for a whole-number input? Check one surviving input by running it forwards.

S046.bridge: The film says the middle team is ahead of the lowest, and the top team is ahead of the middle. Draw every score from the lowest team’s starting line. Which team’s extra bar includes both leads?

S047.bridge: In the film’s twelve theatre rows, pair the outer rows and then move one row in at each end. What does the new front row gain, and what does its partner lose?
S047.recap: To reach term n from term 1, count n − 1 gaps. For a fixed increase, the first and last terms have the same combined value as the next inward pair. With an odd number of terms, count the middle one once.

S050.headline: What does the price difference measure?
S050.intro: A courier charges one fixed collection fee plus a price per kilometre. Comparing two trips cancels the fixed fee. The extra cost pays only for the extra kilometres.

example.prompt: The same courier charges $13 for 4 km and $19 for 7 km. The fixed fee and the price per kilometre are the same on both trips. How much is the fixed fee?
steps: The extra 3 km cost $19 − $13 = $6, so each kilometre costs $2. The 4 km charge accounts for $8 of the shorter trip’s $13 price.
The collection fee is $13 − $8 = $5. In the longer trip, $5 plus 7 lots of $2 makes $19 as required.

S050.bridge: The film doubles the first stationery order to match the two markers in the second. Which pens are left after the matching items cancel? Use the result to rebuild one complete bill.

S051.bridge: In the film, the largest single-day payment that fits the budget may still be unaffordable after earlier days have been paid. Which two consecutive running totals prove the last affordable day?

S052.bridge: In the display puzzle the reading changes, but the gap from 1 follows a simpler rule. In the ladder puzzle, why can a rung above a broken one still have a positive route count?

S053.bridge: A wall replaces one side of the film’s pen. In the fence allowance, which length occurs twice? Find the two neighbouring legal widths that give the same largest area.
S053.recap: First count the sides that actually use the fixed allowance. Write the area in terms of one dimension. Check the eligible dimensions closest to the balance point and explain why moving farther away cannot improve the area.

S054.bridge: In the film’s numbered machine the first move is special. Which state will never be visited again? Start counting five-move laps only after the machine has entered its loop.

S055.bridge: In the five-digit puzzle, start with one choice of the first two digits. Why can both 0 and 9 sometimes work in the centre? Explain how to count that second choice without counting a palindrome twice.

S057.bridge: When the film fixes the even number in box A, test the smallest and largest values for box B. Does each leave an allowed number for C? Explain why a triple cannot appear in two different rows.

S058.bridge: In the film’s final team problem, write down the possible numbers of artists, builders and coders before naming any individuals. What makes the rows of your list alternatives, so their counts can be added?

S059.bridge: The film doubles a whole sum and lines it up with the original. Write the two rows so the matching terms sit above one another. Which two end terms survive the subtraction?

S060.bridge: When both named pairs are adjacent in the film’s final line, how often is that line included in the two single-pair totals? How often should it appear in a count of lines with exactly one adjacent pair?

S061.bridge: Before the film gives its unshaded area, outline the patch shaded twice. If you subtract both shaded areas from the whole board, where must that patch be added back? Then check by counting the unshaded blocks.

S062.bridge: In the film’s list from 1 through 84, follow the number 30. How often does it enter the three single lists, the three pair overlaps and the triple overlap? It should contribute exactly once to the excluded total.

S065.bridge: In the festival puzzle, six rooms book eight helpers each. Circle one helper-room booking. How many bookings does one helper have, and why must the booking total be divided before it can give the number of people?

S066.bridge: When the ruler shifts right, the endpoints and every candidate move together. Later the film lowers the original upper limit to 198. Which previously valid number is just outside that new limit?

S067.bridge: Write the colour pattern for all three rooms in each permitted case. The middle room is red both when all three exhibits are red and when A sits between two blues. In which pattern is exhibit B forbidden?

S069.bridge: The film contrasts a flavour plus a topping with a pair of helpers. In which choice would exchanging the two people change nothing? In the team puzzle, first list the allowed roles by group.

S071.bridge: In the five-painting puzzle, which clues turn Ada, Ben and Chloe into a single block? Test both possible positions of that block against the clue about Eva.

S072.bridge: In the film’s six-stack model, the front and side views each give the tallest stack in a line. For the smallest build, can one tall stack meet two requirements? For the largest, which of the two views limits each position?

S073.bridge: The film gives the top-left and top-right corners. Use the line total and the centre to find their opposite corners. Which row then has only one empty space?
S073.recap: Write the required sum beside the grid. Complete a line with one unknown, then check where that entry also appears. In a magic square, verify both long diagonals as well as every row and column.

S074.bridge: In the film, increasing the width from 8 to 9 also increases the length. Once one rectangle fits the required area, why must every smaller width give too little area and every larger width give too much?

S075.bridge: Before the bead transfer, mark the total number of beads. Decide whether a ratio part still represents the same number after the move. Then compare that argument with the scale factor in the wall drawing.

S078.recap: Colour a square in the overlap. Count how many times your calculation includes it, then check that this matches whether the question asks for painted or unpainted area.

S081.bridge: At the exterior angle, pause and write the sum of the two remote interior angles. In the small triangle formed by the bisectors, mark which halves of that sum you can use.

steps: The row has a line at each end and two grid lines between the cells.
Four vertical lines form three spaces. To draw a rectangle in this row, choose two distinct vertical lines for its sides.

S083.recap: Trace a coloured cell under each required reflection. On a centre line it may have one partner. Away from both centre lines, find all three partners before you count the group.

S085.bridge: The wall replaces one side of the pen. Once the film chooses the end-fence length, calculate the length of the front fence too. Check that all three fenced lengths add to the allowance.

S086.intro: Compare work rates using the same size job and the same length of time. At a steady rate, a machine that needs six minutes for one batch finishes one sixth of it each minute. When two machines work together, add their contributions during the same minute.
S086.bridge: Mark the instant when the leak opens. How much is already in the tank? Only the water still needed is affected by the new filling rate.

S087.recap: For a minimum, show one arrangement that reaches your proposed cube count and produces both views. For a maximum, check each stack against both the row cap and the column cap.

S088.bridge: Start with the alphabetical order of the seven keys. When you subtract the rows with A next to B and then those with C next to D, count how many times that same row disappears.

S089.bridge: Keep your eye on one top corner as the film changes which surfaces receive paint. Then follow its vertical edge down to the bottom corner. Which positions belong together now?

S090.recap: Use cubic units for the volume inside the box. For card area, flatten the base and walls into a net, label their dimensions and decide whether the lid belongs in the total.

S092.bridge: For the two groups, write the count beneath each mean. Which group pulls the combined mean closer to its own? For the eight-day record, mark the day that enters both totals.

S093.recap: Check what the closure removes. At a closed intersection write zero. At a closed edge cross out only the incoming step it blocks, since another step may still reach the same point.

S094.bridge: The two marked cells share a row. After the film counts all rectangles around A, find the last vertical line where a right edge can sit without entering B. Check the direct count against subtraction.

S097.bridge: With the leftmost column empty, draw one horizontal domino in its top row. Look at the square immediately below its left end. Which placement is still possible there, and how many columns does the pair fill?

S099.recap: If a claim joins two conditions with “and”, one false part makes the entire claim false. For the final assignment, check the truth of each complete sentence against its speaker.

example.prompt: On a board with two rows and three columns, start in the middle of the top row. Which cells of the bottom row can you reach in exactly two steps, crossing a full side each time?
steps: To finish in the bottom row after two steps, one move must be down. The other move must be left or right.
The bottom-left and bottom-right cells both work. The bottom-middle cell needs one downward move, and no second move can leave you there.
